body.text: Canada's SR&ED investment tax credit (ITC) under section 127 of the Income Tax Act rewards qualified R&D spending. Most claimants earn a 15% basic rate, while CCPCs and eligible Canadian public corporations earn 35% on up to $6,000,000 yearly for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024; unused credits can be refunded, carried back three years or forward 20.

The Canadian R&D tax landscape underwent its most significant legislative overhaul in over a decade between December 2024 and March 2026, culminating in the Royal Assent of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026. Building upon proposals initially introduced in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (December 16, 2024) and expanded in the 2025 Federal Budget (November 4, 2025), Parliament enacted four foundational reforms to the federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (and for capital property acquired or lease costs first becoming payable after December 15, 2024):

items: Doubling of the Enhanced 35% Expenditure Limit: While the 2024 Fall Economic Statement initially proposed increasing the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3,000,000 to $4,500,000, the 2025 Federal Budget and Bill C-15 doubled the limit from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000, yielding a maximum annual enhanced federal ITC of $2,100,000.

Expansion of Taxable Capital Phase-Out Thresholds: For Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs), the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada phase-out range for the $6,000,000 expenditure limit was widened from the historical $10,000,000–$50,000,000 corridor to $15,000,000–$75,000,000.

Extension of the Enhanced 35% Refundable Credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs): Access to the enhanced 35% ITC on up to $6,000,000 of qualified expenditures was extended beyond CCPCs to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) under amended subsection 127(10.1) and new subsection 127(10.6) of the Income Tax Act, subject to a phase-out based on average annual revenue over the preceding three fiscal years (a revenue-based phase-out method that CCPCs may also elect under subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32)).

Reinstatement of Capital Expenditures and Lease Costs: Reversing the post-2013 repeal of capital eligibility, Bill C-15 reinstated both the Section 37 income deduction and the Section 127 ITC for depreciable capital property (including All or Substantially All [ASA] capital assets and Shared-Use Equipment [SUE]) and equipment lease expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024, with qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs earning 40% partial refundability on enhanced 35% ITCs attributable to capital expenditures.

body.text: Concurrently, on April 1, 2026, the CRA launched its optional SR&ED Pre-Claim Approval regime, providing upfront technical eligibility determinations within eight weeks for businesses with under $25,000,000 in gross business income. At the provincial level, Québec replaced its legacy R&D salary and subcontract tax credits with the unified, 30%/20% refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025—extending provincial tax support to pre-commercialization activities and capital property—while Ontario, British Columbia, and Saskatchewan harmonized their provincial R&D tax credits with the federal capital expenditure and expenditure limit expansions in their 2025 and 2026 budgets.
1. Statutory and Regulatory Architecture of the Federal SR&ED Program

Canada's primary federal mechanism for supporting industrial and academic research and development is the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program. Unlike discretionary grant programs that depend on fixed budgetary envelopes and competitive selection committees, the SR&ED program is an entitlement-based statutory tax incentive enshrined in the federal Income Tax Act (ITA), R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (ITR), C.R.C., c. 945. Provided that a taxpayer's technical activities satisfy the statutory definition of SR&ED under subsection 248(1) of the ITA and its expenditures satisfy the deductibility, qualification, and timely filing rules under sections 37 and 127 of the ITA, the claimant is statutorily entitled to deduct the allowable expenditures and earn the corresponding Investment Tax Credit (ITC).

The program operates through a dual-authority framework within the federal government. The Department of Finance Canada holds legislative policy responsibility for designing and amending the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations, including establishing tax credit rates, expenditure limits, phase-out formulas, and prescribed inclusions or exclusions. The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) administers and enforces the SR&ED program across Canada, and also administers harmonized provincial and territorial R&D tax credits on behalf of participating provinces and territories outside Québec and Alberta. Within the CRA, claims are evaluated jointly by Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs)—who review the scientific and technological eligibility of the claimed projects under subsection 248(1)—and Financial Reviewers (FRs)—who examine accounting records, payroll ledgers, contracts, and tax schedules to verify that claimed costs constitute allowable and qualified expenditures.
1.1 The Dual-Benefit Mechanism: Section 37 Pool Deduction and Section 127 Investment Tax Credit

Under the Canadian federal income tax system, eligible claimants conducting SR&ED in Canada receive two distinct, cumulative fiscal incentives. First, under subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act, a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada accumulates its allowable current SR&ED expenditures (paragraph 37(1)(a)) and eligible post-December 15, 2024 SR&ED capital expenditures (paragraph 37(1)(b)) in a dedicated pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures. The claimant may deduct all or any portion of the positive pool balance to reduce its income for tax purposes in the current taxation year, or carry the undeducted balance forward indefinitely to offset business income in any future taxation year.

Second, under section 127 and section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act, the claimant earns an SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC) calculated at either the 15% basic rate (subsection 127(9)) or the 35% enhanced rate (subsection 127(10.1)) on its "qualified SR&ED expenditures" for the taxation year. Depending on the legal status of the claimant (such as a CCPC, an ECPC, another corporation, an individual sole proprietorship, a partnership, or a trust) and the nature of the expenditure (current versus capital), unused ITCs remaining after offsetting federal Part I tax payable may be refunded in cash at rates of 100% or 40% under section 127.1, or carried back 3 taxation years and carried forward 20 taxation years.
1.2 Statutory Definition of SR&ED: Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act

The statutory foundation of Canadian R&D tax law is the definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. Prior to 1998, this definition was located in section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations; Parliament subsequently moved the definition into subsection 248(1) of the Act without materially changing its substantive meaning.

Under the preamble to the definition in subsection 248(1), SR&ED means a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" and that falls into one of three primary categories of eligible work under paragraphs (a), (b), and (c), accompanied by a fourth category of eligible support work under paragraph (d), and bounded by seven explicit statutory exclusions under paragraphs (e) through (k). Paragraph 248(1)(a) (Basic Research) covers work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view, whereas Paragraph 248(1)(b) (Applied Research) covers work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view.

The vast majority of industrial claims in Canada are filed under Paragraph 248(1)(c) (Experimental Development), which encompasses work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. By expressly including incremental improvements in paragraph (c), Parliament confirmed that a taxpayer does not need to invent a brand-new product category to qualify for SR&ED; incremental enhancements to existing materials, devices, products, or manufacturing processes qualify whenever achieving those improvements requires resolving an underlying technological uncertainty that cannot be removed by standard practice or routine engineering.

In addition, Paragraph 248(1)(d) (Support Work) provides that in applying the definition in respect of a taxpayer, SR&ED includes work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to eight exhaustively enumerated disciplines: (1) engineering, (2) design, (3) operations research, (4) mathematical analysis, (5) computer programming, (6) data collection, (7) testing, or (8) psychological research, where that work is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of basic research, applied research, or experimental development described in paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. Support work is never eligible as SR&ED on its own; its eligibility is strictly derivative and requires demonstrating that the volume and nature of the engineering, programming, testing, or data collection were proportional to and carried out specifically to support core Canadian SR&ED.
1.3 Statutory Exclusions: Paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k)

Even where a taxpayer is engaged in an innovative commercial project, paragraphs (e) through (k) of the definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) explicitly exclude seven categories of "excluded work" that cannot be claimed for tax incentives:

items: Paragraph (e): Market research or sales promotion;
Paragraph (f): Quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products or processes;
Paragraph (g): Research in the social sciences or the humanities;
Paragraph (h): Prospecting, exploring or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum or natural gas;
Paragraph (i): The commercial production of a new or improved material, device or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process;
Paragraph (j): Style changes; and
Paragraph (k): Routine data collection.

body.text: In its Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentives (dated August 13, 2021), the CRA explains that the decisive factor distinguishing eligible support work under paragraph (d) (such as "testing" or "data collection") from excluded work under paragraphs (f) and (k) ("routine testing" or "routine data collection") is the purpose for which the activity was performed. When data collection or testing is carried out specifically to test a scientific or technological hypothesis and resolve a technological uncertainty during SR&ED, it qualifies as support work under paragraph (d); if the same physical test is performed for routine commercial quality control or post-development product verification, it is excluded under paragraph (f) or (k). Similarly, if a mining or energy company conducts SR&ED to develop an experimental extraction technology while simultaneously prospecting for minerals, the eligible experimental development work may be claimed, while all mineral prospecting, exploring, drilling, or production work must be carved out under paragraph (h).
1.4 The CRA's Two-Step "Why and How" Methodology vs. the Five Judicial Criteria

On August 13, 2021, the CRA issued its consolidated Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives, framing the statutory definition in subsection 248(1) around two overarching requirements that must both be met: "Why" the work is conducted and "How" the work is conducted.

The "Why" requirement examines the objective of the work: it must be conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge (in basic or applied research) or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement (in experimental development). The CRA guidelines emphasize that acquiring existing knowledge or know-how that is already available—for example, through employee training, on-the-job learning, hiring expert employees or external consultants, or purchasing proprietary knowledge—does not satisfy the requirement of attempting to achieve a technological advancement. Rather, the work must seek to overcome a scientific or technological uncertainty that cannot be resolved using standard practice or routine engineering available to competent professionals in the field.

The "How" requirement examines the methodology of the work: it must be conducted by means of a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. Under the CRA guidelines, a systematic investigation comprises four sequential operational elements: (1) generating an idea or hypothesis consistent with known facts that serves as a starting point for further investigation toward achieving the objective or resolving the problem; (2) testing that idea or hypothesis by means of experiment or analysis, allowing the hypothesis to evolve and change as a result of testing; (3) developing logical conclusions based on the results or findings of the experiment or analysis; and (4) keeping evidence that is generated as the work progresses.

Importantly, as confirmed by the Tax Court of Canada in Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. The King and the Federal Court of Appeal in Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen (2021 FCA 88), the CRA's administrative "Why and How" articulation does not displace the binding five-question legal test established in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen (98 D.T.C. 1839) and C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada (2001 FCA 393), which remains the controlling legal standard applied by Canadian courts.

body.text: 2. Federal SR&ED Tax Credit Rates, Expenditure Limits, Phase-Outs, and Carryover Rules

A rigorous audit of any Canadian R&D tax report requires distinguishing between the statutory rules applicable to taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024 and the expanded rules enacted by Bill C-15 (Royal Assent March 26, 2026) for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (that is, on or after December 16, 2024). Whether a corporation's taxation year is governed by the former $3,000,000 expenditure limit or the new $6,000,000 expenditure limit depends strictly on the start date of the taxation year rather than its year-end date: a calendar-year corporation whose taxation year began on January 1, 2025 (or January 1, 2026) qualifies for the $6,000,000 expenditure limit, whereas a fiscal-year corporation whose taxation year ran from December 1, 2024 to November 30, 2025 remained subject to the $3,000,000 expenditure limit for that entire fiscal year (while still qualifying to claim capital property acquired and lease costs first becoming payable after December 15, 2024).
2.1 The Two-Tier Federal ITC Rate Structure (35% Enhanced vs. 15% Basic)

The federal SR&ED program operates a two-tier Investment Tax Credit rate structure under section 127 of the Income Tax Act. The Enhanced Rate of 35% consists of the 15% basic rate under subsection 127(9) plus an additional 20% credit under subsection 127(10.1). Prior to December 16, 2024, the 35% enhanced rate was restricted exclusively to Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs). For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 amended subsection 127(10.1) to extend the 35% enhanced rate to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) throughout the taxation year. Both CCPCs and ECPCs earn the 35% enhanced rate on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to their annual Expenditure Limit, which has a maximum ceiling of $6,000,000 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (doubled from $3,000,000 for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024), generating up to $2,100,000 per year in enhanced federal ITCs.

The Basic Rate of 15% under subsection 127(9) applies to all qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred by corporations that are neither CCPCs nor ECPCs (such as foreign-controlled subsidiaries and non-eligible public corporations), as well as to qualified SR&ED expenditures of a CCPC or ECPC that exceed its annual Expenditure Limit for the taxation year. The 15% basic rate also applies to all qualified SR&ED expenditures of individuals (sole proprietorships), beneficiaries of trusts, and members (partners) of a partnership.
2.2 Expenditure Limit Phase-Out Formulas: CCPCs and ECPCs

Associated CCPCs must share the annual $6,000,000 expenditure limit and allocate it among group members using T2 Schedule 49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit) under subsection 127(10.3). Similarly, ECPCs that are members of a consolidated corporate group must share and allocate the $6,000,000 expenditure limit among group members under subsections 127(10.61) and 127(10.62) (with the Minister empowered to allocate the limit under subsection 127(10.63) if the group fails to file an agreement within 30 days of a request). Short taxation years also require prorating the expenditure limit based on the number of days in the taxation year.

For CCPCs that do not elect the revenue method, the annual expenditure limit is phased out under subsection 127(10.2) based on the combined taxable capital employed in Canada of the corporation and its associated group for the immediately preceding taxation year. For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the $3,000,000 expenditure limit began to decrease when prior-year taxable capital reached $10,000,000 and was eliminated ($0) at $50,000,000 (captured on Part 10A of revised T2 Schedule 31). For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit begins to decrease when prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000 and becomes nil ($0) at $75,000,000, in accordance with the following statutory formula:

In this formula, A is nil ($0) when the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC (and its associated group) is $15,000,000 or less; otherwise, A is the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000. Consequently, every $1,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital above $15,000,000 reduces the $6,000,000 expenditure limit by $100,000. Because the federal Small Business Deduction still phases out over the $10,000,000 to $50,000,000 taxable capital range, growing CCPCs must now evaluate the SR&ED phase-out ($15,000,000 to $75,000,000) separately from the small business limit.

For Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)—and for a single CCPC electing under subsection 127(10.31) or an associated group of CCPCs electing together under subsection 127(10.32)—the gradual reduction of the expenditure limit is calculated under subsection 127(10.6) using the average annual revenue of the last 3 fiscal years rather than taxable capital. Under subsection 127(10.6), the variable in the phase-out formula runs on the corporation's (or consolidated/associated group's) three-year average annual revenue exceeding $15,000,000, phasing out the limit at $75,000,000. (Note: In the initial August 2025 draft legislative proposals based on the 2024 Fall Economic Statement, subsection 127(10.6) referenced the proposed $4,500,000 limit; the 2025 Federal Budget and Bill C-15 increased the maximum expenditure limit to $6,000,000 for both CCPCs and ECPCs for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024.)
2.3 Refundability Rules: 100% vs. 40% Cash Refunds (Section 127.1)

When an SR&ED claimant has no federal Part I tax payable (or after its Part I tax payable has been reduced to zero), section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (updated October 7, 2026) govern the extent to which the remaining unclaimed ITC balance can be received as a cash refund.

For any CCPC (whether or not it is a "Qualifying Corporation", provided it is not an excluded corporation) and for any ECPC (for taxation years starting after December 15, 2024), unclaimed ITCs earned at the 35% enhanced rate within the $6,000,000 expenditure limit are 100% refundable on qualified SR&ED expenditures of a current nature and on the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA), and are 40% refundable on qualified SR&ED expenditures of a capital nature (for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024).

Whether a CCPC meets the definition of a "Qualifying Corporation" under section 127.1 determines whether it can also obtain a 40% cash refund on the 15% basic ITC earned on qualified expenditures that exceed its $6,000,000 expenditure limit. A CCPC is a Qualifying Corporation if its taxable income for the prior taxation year (combined with the taxable incomes of all associated corporations) does not exceed its Qualifying Income Limit. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the Qualifying Income Limit is calculated as $500,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000], where A is prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada in excess of $15,000,000 (hitting zero at $75,000,000; for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the formula used $40,000,000 and excess taxable capital over $10,000,000, hitting zero at $50,000,000). If a CCPC is a Qualifying Corporation, 40% of its unclaimed 15% basic ITCs above the expenditure limit is refundable; if a CCPC is not a Qualifying Corporation, 0% of its 15% basic ITCs is refundable. Individuals (sole proprietors) and trusts also receive a 40% refund on their unclaimed 15% basic ITCs (or 100% under specific historical profiles, with CRA guidance confirming 40% refundability on basic 15% credits for individuals after offsetting tax owing). Finally, no ITC refund can be claimed by any taxpayer in respect of ITCs earned on repayments of government/non-government assistance or contract payments.

body.text: 2.4 Carryback, Carryforward, and Loss Restriction Event (Acquisition of Control) Rules

Any portion of an earned SR&ED ITC that is not refunded and is not applied to reduce federal Part I tax in the current taxation year may be carried back up to 3 previous taxation years or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years. A carryback is limited to the earlier taxation year's federal Part I tax remaining after that year's credits, and any ITC amount refunded in cash is deemed to have been applied against Part I tax so that it cannot also be carried back or forward.

By contrast, a positive balance in the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures never expires: it can be carried forward indefinitely as a running balance and deducted in any future taxation year against business income. The sole entity exception is a partnership: because a partnership computes its net income at the partnership level under subsection 96(1) for flow-through allocation to its partners, a partnership cannot carry forward a Section 37 SR&ED pool balance to a subsequent fiscal period and must instead deduct 100% of the pool balance in computing its net business income for the fiscal period in which the expenditures were incurred.

When a corporation undergoes an acquisition of control (or a trust gets a new majority-interest beneficiary, triggering a "loss restriction event"), a deemed taxation year-end occurs immediately before the acquisition of control. Under paragraph 37(1)(h) and subsection 37(6.1) of the Income Tax Act, the corporation's Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures is reduced to nil at that time, and the undeducted pool balance may only be reinstated and carried forward to subsequent taxation years if the business to which the SR&ED expenditures relate continues to be carried on by the corporation for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit. Parallel restrictions govern carrying forward unused ITCs earned prior to an acquisition of control or carrying back unused ITCs earned after an acquisition of control.
2.5 Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credits (Subsections 127(27) to 127(36))

Under subsections 127(27) to 127(36) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, previously earned SR&ED ITCs are subject to recapture whenever a claimant sells property whose cost was included in qualified SR&ED expenditures (such as materials transformed into a prototype or experimental production output, ASA capital property, or Shared-Use Equipment) or converts that property to commercial use. Although paragraph 127(27)(a) contains a textual reference to "the 10 preceding taxation years," statutory transitional rules extended the recapture window so that recapture applies for 20 taxation years from the taxation year in which the ITC was earned.

When recapture is triggered, the recaptured ITC amount is added directly to the taxpayer's federal Part I tax payable for the taxation year of disposition or conversion. For standard SR&ED property, the recapture is the lesser of the ITC originally earned on the property and the applicable ITC percentage multiplied by the proceeds of disposition (if sold at arm's length) or the fair market value (FMV) of the property (if converted to commercial use or transferred to a non-arm's length party under subclause 127(27)(f)(ii)(B)). For Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), because only 25% of the capital cost in the first term and 25% in the second term (up to 50% in total) qualifies for an ITC, SUE is considered converted to commercial use only when its SR&ED usage becomes merely incidental—that is, when all or substantially all (90% or more) of the property is converted to commercial use—and the recapture calculation applies the ITC rate to only 25% (if only first-term SUE was claimed) or 50% (if both first-term and second-term SUE were claimed) of the proceeds of disposition or fair market value. Under paragraphs 37(1)(c.2) and 37(1)(c.3), any SR&ED ITC recaptured in the prior taxation year is added back into the claimant's Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures.
3. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs) and Cost Calculation Methodologies

To be included in the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and the Section 127 pool of qualified SR&ED expenditures, an outlay must first qualify as an expenditure incurred by the claimant on or in respect of SR&ED carried on in Canada under subsection 37(8) of the Income Tax Act and section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations.
3.1 Overhead Election: The Irrevocable Annual Choice Between Proxy and Traditional Methods

Under subsection 37(10) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's Traditional and Proxy Methods Policy, a claimant must select either the Proxy Method or the Traditional Method for each taxation year to calculate its SR&ED expenditures. The election to use the Proxy Method is made by ticking Line 160 in Part 3 of Form T661 when the first SR&ED claim for the taxation year is filed. If the claimant ticks Line 162 (or fails to select a method on Form T661), the Traditional Method applies automatically. Once Form T661 has been filed for a taxation year, the choice of method is irrevocable for that taxation year and cannot be changed on an amended return.

Under the Traditional Method, the claimant must specifically identify, track, allocate, and justify actual SR&ED overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 of Form T661 that are directly attributable (both directly related and incremental) to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada under subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3) of the Income Tax Regulations. These actual overhead expenditures are included in both the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool for ITC purposes.

Under the Proxy Method, the claimant does not track or claim actual SR&ED overhead expenditures on Form T661. Instead, the claimant calculates a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in Part 5 of Form T661 equal to 55% of the salary base of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada (Regulation 2900(4)). The PPA is entered on Line 502 of Form T661 and is included in qualified SR&ED expenditures to earn the 15% or 35% federal ITC, but cannot be included in the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures; instead, the actual overhead expenses represented by the PPA remain deductible as ordinary business expenses under section 9 of the Income Tax Act.

body.text: 3.2 Salaries and Wages (Subsections 248(1), 37(8), 37(9)–(9.3), and 78(4))

Under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025), "salary or wages" means the income of a taxpayer from an office or employment as computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the Act, including fees received for services not rendered in the course of the taxpayer's business, but excluding superannuation or pension benefits and retiring allowances. Allowable SR&ED salary or wages include regular gross pay, cash outlays for taxable benefits, and non-cash taxable benefits (such as automobile benefits, housing/board/meals, gifts/awards, low-interest loans, group term life insurance, or tuition fees), provided the benefit value is a reasonable estimate of actual costs, excludes any GST/HST or PST for which the employer can claim an input tax credit under subsection 248(16), and is not also deducted as a separate business expense. Signing inducements and non-competition payments are also eligible as remuneration for services rendered during employment, and bonuses or remuneration based on profits are eligible solely for employees other than specified employees. Conversely, the employer's share of payroll benefits, extended vacation or sick leave, section 7 stock option benefits, retiring allowances, sales commissions, and unpaid remuneration are excluded from SR&ED salary or wages.

Under the Proxy Method, only the salary or wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada (hands-on technical work) may be claimed. Under the Traditional Method (Regulation 2900(2)(b)), the claimant may include salary or wages of employees who directly undertake SR&ED (direct performance of basic/applied research or experimental development by personnel with a technological background, including direct technological planning or contract administration), supervise SR&ED (technical supervision of employees undertaking or supporting SR&ED by a supervisor with technological expertise), or support SR&ED (performing paragraph 248(1)(d) technical support work, excluding clerical duties).

The portion of an employee's salary or wages allocated to SR&ED is calculated using a time-based ratio of the time spent on SR&ED relative to total time worked in the taxation year. For example, if a salaried employee earning $100,000 per year spends all 1,800 regular hours directly engaged in SR&ED and works 600 hours of unpaid overtime on general administrative work, the allowable SR&ED salary portion is $75,000 (1,800 ÷ 2,400 × $100,000). Under the All or Substantially All (ASA — 90% Rule) in subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I) and Regulation 2900(5), if an employee spends 90% or more of their working time over the entire taxation year on the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, 100% of their eligible salary or wages for the year is deemed to relate to SR&ED (subject to specified employee caps and bonus restrictions). If an employee earning $100,000 spends 90% of their time on SR&ED for the first 6 months and 0% for the remaining 6 months, their full-year ratio is 45% ($45,000), and the 90% ASA rule does not apply.

A "specified employee" is defined in subsection 248(1) as an employee who does not deal at arm's length with the employer or who owns, directly or indirectly, a specified threshold of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation (such as a sole or controlling shareholder; while the CRA policy table of contents references the 10% share ownership threshold in section 6.0, the exact statutory subsection 248(1) definition applies). Specified employees are governed by three statutory restrictions:

items: Ineligibility of Bonuses and Profit-Based Remuneration (Subsection 37(9)): Under subsection 37(9) of the Income Tax Act, any bonus or remuneration based on profits paid or payable to a specified employee is excluded from SR&ED expenditures. However, under an administrative exception in Section 6.1 of the CRA SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, if a corporation was unable to pay a regular salary throughout the year and a specified employee's only remuneration in the year for performing SR&ED duties was a year-end lump-sum bonus or profit-based payment (with all required payroll procedures and source deductions applied), the CRA will treat an amount commensurate with the performance of those SR&ED duties (determined using industrial standards published by technological or professional associations) as eligible regular salary or wages for both the Section 37 pool and the PPA calculation.

Maximum SR&ED Salary Cap — 5 Times YMPE (Subsection 37(9.1)): Under clauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) and (B) and subsection 37(9.1) of the ITA, the maximum allowable SR&ED salary or wages of a specified employee is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan, prorated for the number of days in the taxation year on which the individual was a specified employee.

Associated Corporation Allocation — Form T1174 (Subsection 37(9.3)): If a specified employee works for two or more associated corporations (including deemed associated individuals or partnerships), no SR&ED salary may be claimed by any of the corporations unless they file Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)) together with a certified copy of the directors' resolution authorizing the agreement, and the total allocated across all associated corporations cannot exceed 5 times the YMPE.

body.text: For SR&ED work carried on outside Canada, subsection 37(1.5) permits claiming on Line 307 of Form T661 the lesser of Amount A (actual salary paid to the employee for SR&ED work carried on outside Canada) and Amount B (10% of the total SR&ED salary or wages claimed for SR&ED carried on in Canada). For example, if a company has total SR&ED salaries of $540,000, of which $45,000 was paid to an employee performing SR&ED outside Canada for 5 months and $495,000 was for SR&ED in Canada, Amount B is 10% of $495,000 ($49,500); because Amount A ($45,000) is less than $49,500, the full $45,000 is allowable on Line 307.

Finally, under subsection 78(4) of the Income Tax Act, any employee remuneration that is not paid within 180 days from the end of the taxation year in which the expense was incurred is deemed not to have been incurred in that taxation year. If subsequently paid in a later taxation year, it may be claimed on Line 310 of Form T661 in the year of payment, but is permanently excluded from the PPA salary base under Regulation 2900(9). Similarly, non-salary current SR&ED expenditures unpaid 180 days after year-end must be deducted from qualified expenditures on Line 520 of Form T661 until the taxation year in which they are paid (Line 500).
3.3 Overhead Calculations: The 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) vs. Traditional Method Tests

When a claimant elects the Proxy Method, the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is calculated in Part 5 of Form T661 as 55% of the salary base (Regulation 2900(4); prior to 2014, the rate was 65% for 2012 and earlier years and 60% for 2013). Under Regulation 2900(9), the Salary Base (Line 818) starts with the salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada (Line 810) and excludes (on Line 812): (1) taxable benefits, (2) bonuses, (3) remuneration based on profits, (4) section 7 stock options, and (5) prior-year unpaid wages paid in the current year (Line 310).
Furthermore, for each specified employee, Regulation 2900(7) restricts the amount that can be included in the PPA salary base (Lines 850 to 860) to the lesser of:

items: The specified employee's directly engaged Canadian SR&ED salary or wages (Total salary excluding bonuses, profit-based remuneration, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages on Line 852 multiplied by % of SR&ED time on Line 854 = Line 856);
75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages (both SR&ED and non-SR&ED) for the year, excluding bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages; and

2.5 × A × (B ÷ 365) (Line 858), where A is the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, and B is the number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual (with no proration for days the employee was not a specified employee; for example, in an illustrative historical year where the YMPE was $55,300, 2.5 × $55,300 equalled $138,250).

body.text: Under Regulation 2900(6), the resulting 55% PPA is also subject to an overall cap calculated by the formula A − B − C, where A is the total of all amounts deducted in computing net income for tax purposes from the business for the year (including cost of goods sold), and B and C represent deducted SR&ED pool amounts and specific non-overhead items prescribed in Regulation 2900(6).

When a claimant uses the Traditional Method, overhead and other expenditures claimed on Line 360 under paragraph 2900(2)(c) of the Income Tax Regulations must pass two cumulative tests set out in the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy (updated October 14, 2022):

items: The "Directly Related" Test: The expenditure must link directly—without any intervening step or intermediary—to (a) the SR&ED work, (b) the SR&ED staff, or (c) the machinery or equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED in Canada.
The "Incremental" Test: The expenditure (or claimed portion thereof) would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED not occurred.

body.text: Under these tests, fixed monthly telephone or internet charges fail the incremental test because they are ordinary business expenses incurred regardless of SR&ED, whereas identifiable long-distance charges directly related and incremental to SR&ED may qualify. Similarly, a fixed-cost maintenance contract generally fails the incremental test, whereas variable maintenance and upkeep of SR&ED premises, facilities, or equipment under paragraph 2900(3)(a) is allowable based on the reasonable portion allocated to SR&ED (for example, if 25% of a $10,000 variable maintenance contract [$2,500] relates to dual-use equipment that is used 40% of its operating time for SR&ED, 40% of $2,500 = $1,000 is an allowable SR&ED overhead expenditure). Waste disposal costs incurred after the SR&ED activity has finished do not qualify because they are not incurred during the prosecution of SR&ED. Furthermore, even if directly related and incremental, prescribed expenditures under Regulation 2902—such as costs to attend technical conventions or conferences (clause 2902(a)(i)(F)), interest on borrowed money (clause 2902(a)(i)(C)), society membership dues, and legal or accounting fees including SR&ED claim preparation fees (clause 2902(a)(i)(B))—cannot be claimed.
3.4 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed (Regulation 2900(2)(a) and Subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V))

Under both the Traditional Method and the Proxy Method, a claimant may include 100% of the cost of materials consumed or materials transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. According to the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy (updated March 27, 2026), "materials for SR&ED" must be physical, tangible items (in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) that at a given moment in the SR&ED process compose the body of a tangible object on which SR&ED is carried out or that results from the SR&ED. For purchased merchandise or raw materials, the allowable cost is the laid-down cost (invoice cost, customs and excise duties, transportation, other acquisition costs, and storage costs to bring the item to the SR&ED location); for manufactured inventories, it is the production cost or industrial cost price (laid-down cost of materials, direct labour costs, and the share of production overhead properly chargeable to production, even if the claimant uses the Proxy Method). Materials can be purchased from Canadian or foreign suppliers, but can only be claimed in the taxation year in which they are actually consumed or transformed in SR&ED in Canada (and must be paid within 180 days of year-end to earn an ITC in that year).

Materials consumed are materials destroyed, used up, or rendered virtually valueless as a result of SR&ED (such as ink consumed in printing tests, cardboard boxes rendered valueless during testing and placed in a recycling bin, or wood, chemicals, and metal parts destroyed during testing). Materials transformed are materials physically changed or incorporated into another product or experimental production run (ED+EP) during SR&ED without being rendered virtually valueless (such as yarn converted into fabric during an eligible experimental production run or wood treated with an experimental chemical that retains value). Labour, overhead, and material costs relating to excess production (production beyond what is reasonably required for SR&ED) or commercial production are not allowable, and if materials transformed are later sold or converted to commercial use within 20 years, they trigger ITC recapture under subsections 127(27) to (36).
3.5 Subcontractors (Arm's Length vs. Non-Arm's Length) and Third-Party Payments

When a claimant engages an arm's length contractor to perform SR&ED in Canada on its behalf (Line 340 of Form T661), the SR&ED work is controlled by the payer, intellectual property rights are exclusive to the payer, and the contract is accounted for on an accrual basis. While 100% of an eligible arm's length SR&ED contract expenditure enters the Section 37 deductible pool, only 80% of the contract expenditure qualifies for the Section 127 ITC (with the remaining 20% deducted on Line 529 of Form T661). Furthermore, to qualify for an ITC, the contractor must be a Canadian taxable supplier (amounts paid to a non-taxable supplier, such as a foreign contractor without a Canadian permanent establishment, are deducted on Line 528). To prevent both the payer and the contractor from claiming ITCs on the same work, the contractor must deduct the contract payment received from the Canadian taxable supplier (or from a Canadian government, municipality, public authority, or tax-exempt entity, except for prescribed Canadian Commercial Corporation amounts under Regulation 4606) from its own qualified expenditures under subsection 127(18).

When SR&ED is performed on behalf of a claimant by a non-arm's length (NAL) contractor (Line 345), the payment is excluded from the payer's direct qualified expenditures for ITC purposes (deducted in full on Line 541). Instead, the NAL performer and the payer may jointly file Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) under subsection 127(13) to transfer all or part of the performer's qualified SR&ED expenditures (including its PPA) to the payer (added on Line 508 of the payer's T661 and deducted on Line 540 of the performer's T661). Additionally, under subsection 127(11.6), when a claimant purchases goods, materials, or non-SR&ED services (including post-December 15, 2024 equipment leases) from a non-arm's length supplier, the qualified expenditure for ITC purposes is capped at the NAL supplier's adjusted selling cost (for goods) or adjusted service cost (for services), with any intercompany markup deducted on Line 542.

A Third-Party Payment (Line 370 of Form T661) is a payment made to a qualifying Canadian entity to be used for SR&ED carried on in Canada that relates to a business of the claimant, where the claimant is entitled to exploit the results on a non-exclusive, preferential basis. Only 80% of a third-party payment qualifies for an ITC (20% deducted on Line 529), and the claimant must complete and attach a separate Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)) for each payment. Under the CRA's Third-Party Payments Policy, eligible recipients are classified as Entity A (a corporation resident in Canada under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.1), claimable in the year the SR&ED is performed), Entity B (an approved association under clause 37(1)(a)(ii)(A)), Entity C (an approved university, college, or research institute under clause 37(1)(a)(ii)(B)), Entity D (a paragraph 149(1)(j) non-profit SR&ED corporation resident in Canada spending at least 90% of its income on Canadian SR&ED), Entity E (an approved granting council such as NSERC, CIHR, or SSHRC funding a B, C, or D entity under clause 37(1)(a)(ii)(E); payments to Entities B through E are claimable in the year paid, including eligible agricultural producer check-off dues), and Entity F (a paragraph 149(1)(j) non-profit SR&ED corporation funded by a corporate claimant for basic or applied research under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(iii)).
3.6 Reinstatement of Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Lease Costs After December 15, 2024

Following the enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, capital expenditures on depreciable property acquired (and available for use) after December 15, 2024 and equipment lease costs first becoming payable after December 15, 2024 once again qualify for SR&ED tax incentives (whereas capital and lease expenditures incurred between January 1, 2014 and December 15, 2024 remain ineligible).

Under the CRA's SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (updated June 29, 2026), an expenditure to acquire new or used depreciable property (other than a building or leasehold interest in a building, or non-depreciable land) after December 15, 2024 qualifies as an SR&ED capital expenditure on Line 390 of Form T661 (paragraph 37(1)(b)) if, at the time of acquisition, the claimant intended that either (1) the property would be used during all or substantially all (ASA — 90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, or (2) ASA (90% or more) of its value would be consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Under the Proxy Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(III)), General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF) (desks, chairs, filing cabinets, lamps, photocopiers, fax machines, telephones, and calculators—note that computers, hardware, software, and ancillary equipment are NOT considered GPOEF) is excluded from ASA capital expenditures, whereas under the Traditional Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III)), GPOEF used ≥90% in SR&ED is eligible. Because deducting an SR&ED capital expenditure from the Section 37 pool is deemed to be Capital Cost Allowance (CCA), property claimed on Line 390 must not be included on T2 Schedule 8 (CCA). Furthermore, while used equipment meeting the 90% ASA test can enter the Section 37 deductible pool on Line 390, used equipment is a prescribed expenditure under Regulation 2902 and is subtracted in Part 4 of Form T661 so that only new depreciable property earns a Section 127 ITC.

If new depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 does not meet the 90% ASA test because it is used for both SR&ED and commercial production, its capital cost is depreciated under regular CCA rules on T2 Schedule 8 (not in the Section 37 pool), but it may earn a Section 127 ITC on Line 504 of Form T661 as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) under subsection 127(9) and the CRA's SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (updated May 22, 2026). To qualify as First-Term SUE, the property must be (1) new depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, (2) not GPOEF, (3) not Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under Regulation 2900(11) (which excludes buildings, equipment used for assembling/commissioning a commercial plant under para. 2900(11)(c), and property intended at acquisition to be used primarily [<50% SR&ED] for non-SR&ED over its expected useful life under para. 2900(11)(d)), and (4) actually used primarily (more than 50% but less than 90%) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada during the First Period (from acquisition until the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after acquisition). To qualify as Second-Term SUE, the property must have qualified as First-Term SUE and be actually used primarily (more than 50%) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada during the Second Period (from acquisition until the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after acquisition). For both the Proxy and Traditional methods, 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost of the equipment qualifies for the ITC as First-Term SUE and an additional 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost qualifies as Second-Term SUE.

Under the CRA's SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (updated June 8, 2026), lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 for equipment used in SR&ED in Canada (excluding building rent under subparagraph 37(8)(d)(ii), unless a prescribed special-purpose building approved by the Department of Finance) qualify as current expenditures. Under the Proxy Method, leased equipment (excluding GPOEF) used ASA (90% or more) in SR&ED in the year is 100% claimable on Line 350 (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I)); leased equipment (excluding GPOEF) used primarily (more than 50% to less than 90%) in SR&ED is 50% claimable on Line 355 (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI)); and leased equipment used 50% or less in SR&ED is 0% claimable. Under the Traditional Method, leased equipment (including GPOEF) used ASA (90% or more) is 100% claimable on Line 350 (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)), and leased equipment used less than 90% is claimable proportionally to its SR&ED usage percentage as overhead on Line 360 if directly related and incremental (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) and Regulation 2900(2)(c)). Crucially, in Section 4.3.1 of the June 8, 2026 SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy, the CRA applies the Tax Court of Canada precedent in Data Kinetics Ltd. v. The Queen (98 D.T.C. 1877) to confirm that costs incurred after December 15, 2024 for dedicated telecommunications bandwidth and external mainframe/compute time made available through sophisticated optoelectronic and computer equipment qualify as an eligible lease of equipment (not GPOEF) even under the Proxy Method, provided the bandwidth/compute is dedicated to SR&ED.
4. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes

Seven Canadian provinces and one territory offer dedicated provincial or territorial R&D tax credits, while Alberta offers the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG). Except for Québec (administered by Revenu Québec) and Alberta (administered by Alberta Corporate Income Tax / Tax and Revenue Administration), all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits are administered by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) via the T2 Corporation Income Tax Return (or T1 Individual return in Newfoundland and Labrador and Yukon) and mirror the federal definition of SR&ED under subsection 248(1). Prince Edward Island, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut do not offer provincial or territorial R&D tax credits.
4.1 Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, OBRITC, and Transitional Credits

Corporations with a permanent establishment in Ontario may claim three distinct R&D tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), all administered by the CRA. First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) (Section 96, Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), claimed on T2 Schedule 566) is an 8% fully refundable tax credit for taxation years commencing after May 31, 2016 (10% prior to June 1, 2016) on up to $3,000,000 of qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures per year (shared among associated corporations), providing a maximum annual refund of $240,000. The $3,000,000 OITC expenditure limit is gradually reduced when the associated group's prior-year federal taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000, or when its prior-year taxable capital is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000. Following federal Bill C-15, Ontario updated the OITC (as reflected in the October 30, 2026 Ontario guidance and 2026 Fall Statement) so that qualified expenditures include 100% of current expenditures and 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024 (capital expenditures between January 1, 2014 and December 15, 2024 were excluded, while pre-2014 capital expenditures were included at 40%). The OITC is not subject to recapture and may be waived in writing.

Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC) (Section 38 / Section 95, Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), claimed on T2 Schedule 508) is a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit for taxation years starting after May 31, 2016 (4.5% prior to June 1, 2016) with no expenditure cap, available to all corporations carrying on SR&ED through an Ontario permanent establishment (and updated in the 2026 Ontario Fall Statement to include post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures). Unused ORDTC credits can be carried back 3 years and carried forward 20 years, are subject to recapture, and may be waived in writing by the corporation (for example, to prevent an unutilized non-refundable credit from reducing the federal SR&ED pool as government assistance).

Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC) (Section 97, Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), claimed on T2 Schedule 568 with Schedule 569 filed for each contract) is a 20% fully refundable tax credit on qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred under eligible contracts with Eligible Research Institutes (ERIs) in Ontario, subject to a $20,000,000 annual expenditure cap per associated group (maximum annual refund of $4,000,000) and no recapture. A fourth administrative schedule, Ontario Transitional Tax Debits and Credits (T2 Schedule 506 and Schedule 507), tracks transitional adjustments for pre-2009 SR&ED pools.
4.2 Québec: The 2025–2026 CRIC Overhaul vs. Legacy R&D Credits

Québec administers its own corporate tax system through Revenu Québec under the Taxation Act (Québec), with corporations claiming their Québec R&D income deduction on Form RD-222-V (Deduction Respecting Scientific Research and Experimental Development Expenditures), while the CRA conducts the scientific review of R&D work under federal-provincial harmonization.

For taxation years (or partnership fiscal periods) beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec replaced its legacy R&D tax credit suite with the unified Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), claimed on Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (accompanied by Form RD-1029.8.EN-T for associated corporation limit agreements and Form RD-1029.8.PR-T for pre-commercialization activities). The CRIC provides a 100% refundable tax credit equal to 30% on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures above the applicable exclusion threshold, and 20% on all qualified expenditures exceeding the $1,000,000 limit. Uniquely in Canada, the CRIC covers both traditional R&D (basic research, applied research, and experimental development) and eligible pre-commercialization activities undertaken in Québec in conjunction with R&D work carried out in Québec by or on behalf of the corporation—specifically (1) tests, technological validations, and studies to meet regulatory requirements and obtain an initial approval or certification for commercializing an innovation, (2) product design (development of form and aesthetics, improved functionality, and choice of materials), and (3) implementation of a quality control system required to obtain initial approval or certification.

Qualified CRIC expenditures comprise 100% of salaries and wages paid to the corporation's employees, 50% of amounts paid to a subcontractor for a contract carried out in Québec, 50% of payments made to an eligible public research centre, eligible research consortium, or eligible university entity, and 100% of property acquisition costs (capital property) other than land, buildings, or rights to use land or buildings (provided the property is not claimed under the Québec Tax Credit for Investment and Innovation [C3i] or a Large Investment Project tax holiday). Qualified expenditures in the taxation year must exceed an annual exclusion threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the basic personal amount of the applicable personal income tax system for each employee, adjusted to reflect the proportion of time spent by each employee on eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities.

For taxation years beginning on or before March 25, 2025, Québec's legacy refundable R&D tax credits apply (with Revenu Québec having cancelled general guide IN-109-V in favour of corporate guide CO-17.G): Form RD-1029.7-V (Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D), with Form RD-1029.7.8-T for associated corporations), Form RD-1029.8.6-V (Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium), Form RD-1029.8.9.03-V (Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium), and Form RD-1029.8.16.1-V (Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research), which provided refundable credits ranging from 14% to 30% (historically 17.5% to 37.5% or 35% prior to June 5, 2014) on up to $3,000,000 of eligible expenditures for the enhanced rate.
4.3 British Columbia, Alberta, Prairie, Atlantic, and Territorial Regimes

In British Columbia, the BC SR&ED Tax Credit (Part 6, Sections 98 to 102.6, British Columbia Income Tax Act, claimed on Form T666 within 18 months of year-end and reported on T2 Schedule 5, Line 674 for refundable and Line 659 for non-refundable) was amended in the February 17, 2026 BC Budget to make the credit permanent effective April 16, 2026, align with the federal capital expenditure restoration, expand the 10% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) alongside CCPCs for taxation years starting after December 15, 2024, and double the annual expenditure limit for the 10% refundable credit from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 (yielding up to $600,000 in refundable BC credits, determined under federal subsections 127(10.2) and 127(10.6)). Non-CCPCs/non-ECPCs, corporate partners of partnerships, and CCPC/ECPC expenditures above the expenditure limit earn a 10% non-refundable credit that carries back 3 years and forward 10 years (or may be renounced under subsection 100(1) of the BC ITA), and BC applies a 10-year recapture rule (sections 102.1 to 102.6, reported on Schedule 5, Line 241).

In Alberta, for expenditures incurred after December 31, 2020 (replacing the former 10% Alberta SR&ED tax credit that ended December 31, 2019), the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) (claimed on AT1 Schedule 29 and Form AT4970 under Information Circular IEG-1 within 15 months after the corporation's AT1 filing-due date) provides a refundable payment/credit on up to $4,000,000 in annual Alberta R&D spending matching federal SR&ED eligible expenditures: an 8% base payment on eligible spending up to the corporation's base level of spending (calculated as the corporation's average qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the previous 2 years), and an enhanced 20% payment on eligible Alberta R&D spending that exceeds the 2-year average base spending level.

In Saskatchewan, under the March 18, 2026 Saskatchewan Budget, the 10% Saskatchewan R&D Tax Credit (T2 Schedule 403, The Saskatchewan Income Tax Act, 2000, s. 63.4) was expanded retroactive to December 16, 2024 to include capital expenditures for all corporations and to double the annual qualifying expenditure limit for the 10% refundable credit for CCPCs from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000 (for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024; reported on Schedule 5, Line 645). Expenditures above the $2,000,000 limit and expenditures by non-CCPCs earn a 10% non-refundable credit (Schedule 5, Line 631), subject to an overall yearly maximum credit limit of $1,000,000 (combined refundable and non-refundable), with unused non-refundable credits carrying back 3 years and forward 10 years, no recapture, and an election to renounce under subsection 63.4(13).

In Manitoba, the Manitoba R&D Tax Credit (T2 Schedule 380) equals 15% of eligible Manitoba expenditures (reduced from 20% after April 11, 2017): for in-house R&D, one-half (7.5%) is refundable and one-half (7.5%) is non-refundable (carrying back 3 years and forward 20 years), whereas for R&D carried on under contract with a qualifying Manitoba institution, 100% (15%) is refundable, with no cap and no recapture. In Nova Scotia (T2 Schedule 340), New Brunswick (T2 Schedule 360), and Newfoundland and Labrador (T2 Schedule 301 for corporations; Form T1129 for individuals), the provincial R&D tax credit is 15% fully refundable with no cap (Nova Scotia and New Brunswick apply recapture; Newfoundland and Labrador has no recapture). Finally, Yukon (T2 Schedule 442 for corporations; Form T1232 for individuals) provides a 15% fully refundable credit plus an additional 5% refundable credit (20% total) on amounts paid or payable to Yukon University (formerly Yukon College), with no cap and no recapture.

body.text: 5. Interaction with Government Assistance, Grants, and Stacking Mechanics
5.1 Statutory Definitions and Reduction Rules for Government and Non-Government Assistance

Under subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, "government assistance" means assistance from a government, municipality, or other public authority (including Crown corporations and foreign governments) in the form of a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, investment allowance, or any other form of assistance, other than the federal SR&ED ITC itself. Provincial and territorial R&D tax credits (unless renounced/waived on or before the filing-due date) and direct R&D grants such as the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) constitute government assistance. "Non-government assistance" means an amount that would be included in income under paragraph 12(1)(x) of the Act as an inducement, reimbursement, contribution, or allowance for the cost of property or an outlay or expense.

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18) of the Income Tax Act, any government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payment that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before its income tax return filing-due date reduces both the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures (except for contract payments, which reduce only qualified expenditures) and the Section 127 pool of qualified SR&ED expenditures (reported on Lines 513 to 518 of Form T661). Assistance allocated to a specific project reduces qualified expenditures only for that project (capped at total project expenditures for the year, with any unapplied excess carried forward to reduce that project's expenditures in subsequent years), and non-arm's length groups may allocate excess assistance using Form T1145 under subsection 127(20). When a claimant repays government or non-government assistance that previously reduced its SR&ED pool, the repayment increases the Section 37 pool under paragraph 37(1)(c) and earns a non-refundable ITC under subsections 127(10.7) and 127(10.8) at the ITC rate from the year the assistance originally applied. Furthermore, under paragraph 37(1)(e) and paragraphs 12(1)(t) and 12(1)(v), federal SR&ED ITCs claimed or refunded in a taxation year reduce the Section 37 pool in the following taxation year (or are included in business income if the pool is reduced below zero), and the portion of provincial/territorial R&D tax credits attributable to the Prescribed Proxy Amount (which does not enter the Section 37 pool) is included directly in net income for tax purposes on T2 Schedule 1 under paragraph 12(1)(x) in the year received.
5.2 The Proxy Method Salary Base Advantage When Stacking NRC IRAP Grants and Worked Examples

When a claimant receives a salary-based grant such as NRC IRAP and elects the Proxy Method, the IRAP grant is subtracted from qualified expenditures on Line 515 in Part 4 of Form T661. However, under Regulation 2900(4) and Part 5 of Form T661, the Salary Base (Line 818) used to calculate the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (Line 502) is computed on the full gross eligible SR&ED salaries incurred before subtracting government assistance.
To illustrate how federal SR&ED, provincial R&D tax credits, and NRC IRAP grants interact in practice, consider the following mathematical examples based on the CRA's published calculation rules:

items: Example 1 — Federal CCPC Claim Under the Proxy Method (No Provincial Credit or Grant): A Qualifying CCPC with a taxation year beginning after December 15, 2024 (full $6,000,000 expenditure limit available) elects the Proxy Method and incurs $400,000 in directly engaged SR&ED salaries (which also forms its Salary Base), $30,000 in materials consumed, and $100,000 in arm's length Canadian SR&ED contracts. Its Section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool is $530,000 ($400,000 salaries + $30,000 materials + $100,000 contract, as the proxy amount is not an SR&ED deduction). For Section 127 ITC purposes, its qualified SR&ED expenditures comprise $400,000 (salaries) + $30,000 (materials) + $80,000 (80% of the $100,000 arm's length contract) + $220,000 (55% PPA on the $400,000 salary base) = $730,000. At the 35% enhanced rate, the corporation earns a 100% refundable federal ITC of $255,500 ($730,000 × 35%).

Example 2 — Ontario CCPC Stacking OITC, ORDTC, Federal SR&ED, and an NRC IRAP Grant: An Ontario CCPC (within the $3,000,000 OITC limit and $6,000,000 federal limit) incurs $200,000 in qualifying salaries, $50,000 in arm's length subcontractor payments (80% = $40,000 eligible), and $10,000 in materials consumed, and elects the Proxy Method, adding a 55% PPA of $110,000 (55% of $200,000) for a gross SR&ED pool of $360,000 ($260,000 actual cash outlay). On the $360,000 base, the standalone 8% Ontario OITC is $28,800 ($360,000 × 8%, refundable) and the 3.5% Ontario ORDTC is $12,600 on the unadjusted base (or $11,592 after reducing the ORDTC base by the $28,800 OITC). If the corporation waives the non-refundable ORDTC and deducts only the $28,800 refundable OITC as provincial government assistance on Line 513 of Form T661, its net federal qualified SR&ED expenditures are $331,200 ($360,000 − $28,800), generating a 35% refundable federal ITC of $115,920 and a combined cash refund of $144,720 ($28,800 OITC + $115,920 federal ITC = 55.66% of the $260,000 cash outlay). If the same corporation also receives a $100,000 NRC IRAP salary grant, the 55% PPA remains $110,000 (calculated on the $200,000 gross salary base), while the $100,000 IRAP grant reduces the pool from $360,000 to $260,000, yielding an 8% OITC of $20,800 ($260,000 × 8%), net federal qualified expenditures of $239,200 ($260,000 − $20,800), and a 35% federal ITC of $83,720—for a total cash recovery of $204,520 ($100,000 IRAP + $20,800 OITC + $83,720 federal ITC = 78.66% of the $260,000 cash outlay).

Example 3 — Québec CCPC Stacking the New CRIC and Federal SR&ED (Including Capital Property): A Québec CCPC whose taxation year begins on January 1, 2026 (after March 25, 2025) incurs $200,000 in Québec R&D salaries and $100,000 in new ASA R&D capital equipment in Québec ($300,000 total outlay), where the applicable CRIC exclusion threshold is the $50,000 floor. Its net qualified CRIC expenditures are $250,000 ($300,000 − $50,000), earning a 30% refundable Québec CRIC of $75,000 ($50,000 attributable to salaries and $25,000 attributable to capital property). Federally under the Proxy Method, its net current qualified expenditures are $260,000 ($200,000 salaries + $110,000 PPA − $50,000 CRIC on salaries), earning a 100% refundable 35% federal ITC of $91,000, and its net capital qualified expenditures are $75,000 ($100,000 capital cost − $25,000 CRIC on capital), earning a 35% federal ITC of $26,250 (of which 40% = $10,500 is refunded in cash and 60% = $15,750 is non-refundable)—for total combined federal and Québec tax credits of $192,250 (64.08% of the $300,000 cash outlay).

The complete inventory of prescribed federal SR&ED forms—including the May 2026 post-Bill C-15 revisions—is presented below:
