body.text: 6.2 Structural Breakdown of Form T661 (Parts 1 to 10 — May 15, 2026 Revision)
Form T661 (explained in Guide T4088) is organized into ten parts:

items: Part 1 — General Information: Captures the business name, taxation year, and Business Number.

Part 2 — Project Information: Completed separately for each claimed project. Section A records project identification, including Lines 212 and 214 (Pre-Claim Approval checkbox and case number), Lines 262 and 263 (names of the 10 most expensive post-December 15, 2024 SR&ED capital properties acquired and claimed on Line 390 for the project), Line 266 (whether SR&ED was carried out on behalf of another party), and Lines 267 and 268 (individuals or companies performing SR&ED work who are not employees). Section B contains the three written technical narratives (Lines 242, 244, and 246), and Section C records the supporting evidence maintained for the project.

Part 3 — Calculation of SR&ED Expenditures: Elects the Proxy Method (Line 160) or Traditional Method (Line 162), totals allowable expenditures—including Salaries/Wages (Lines 300–315), Materials Consumed/Transformed (Lines 320/325), Arm's Length Contracts (Line 340), Non-Arm's Length Contracts (Line 345), Equipment Lease Costs incurred after December 15, 2024 (Lines 350 and 355), Traditional Method Overhead (Line 360), Third-Party Payments (Line 370), and ASA Capital Expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024 (Line 390)—and calculates the Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures (including CCA recapture deductions on Line 440, current-year deduction claimed on Line 460, and the pool balance carried forward to future years on Line 470).

Part 4 — Calculation of Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for Investment Tax Credit (ITC) Purposes: Adds prior-year unpaid amounts paid in the year (Line 500), the Prescribed Proxy Amount (Line 502), Shared-Use Equipment (Line 504), and NAL transferred expenditures (Line 508), and subtracts provincial government assistance (Lines 513–517), other government assistance (Line 515), non-government assistance and contract payments, non-salary current expenditures unpaid after 180 days (Line 520), payments to non-taxable suppliers (Line 528), 20% of Line 340 arm's length contracts and Line 370 third-party payments (Line 529), Regulation 2902 prescribed expenditures including used equipment (Line 530), other deductions related to post-December 15, 2024 depreciable property (Line 535), and non-arm's length transfers/adjustments (Lines 540, 541, and 542).

Part 5 — Calculation of Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA): Completed only if Line 160 was ticked; computes the Salary Base (Section A, Lines 810 to 860 and Line 818) and the 55% PPA (Section B, Line 820).

Part 6 — Project Costs: Part 6A breaks down project costs project-by-project (including Line 750 project numbers and Box 759 post-December 15, 2024 leased equipment costs matching Lines 350 + 355); Part 6B (Boxes 780, 782, and 786) reports the 20 most expensive post-December 15, 2024 ASA capital expenditures; and Part 6C (Boxes 788, 790, 792, 794, and 796) reports the 20 most expensive post-December 15, 2024 Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) expenditures (25% of capital cost, coded "1" for first-term SUE or "2" for second-term SUE).
Part 7 — Additional Information: Collects R&D expenditure data for Statistics Canada.
Part 8 — Claim Checklist: Confirms claim completeness before submission.
Part 9 — Claim Preparer Information: Discloses any person or firm paid to prepare or assist in preparing the claim; a $1,000 penalty may be assessed if details are missing or inaccurate.
Part 10 — Certification: Authorized certification signature and date.

body.text: 6.3 The Optional SR&ED Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026) and FTCAS

Launched on April 1, 2026 (replacing earlier pre-claim consultation and review pilots), the CRA's optional SR&ED Pre-Claim Approval process enables businesses to obtain an upfront determination within 8 weeks on whether their planned projects meet the statutory definition of SR&ED before starting work or incurring significant costs. To qualify for Pre-Claim Approval, the business must (1) operate in Canada as a CCPC, other Canadian corporation, or partnership, (2) have less than $25,000,000 in annual gross business income, and (3) be in good standing with the CRA, while the planned project (up to a maximum of 3 projects per application) must not have been included in a previous SR&ED claim and must not involve issues currently under objection or litigation.
The Pre-Claim Approval workflow follows five sequential steps:

items: Request a Case Number: The business confirms eligibility on Canada.ca and requests a Pre-Claim Approval case number (delivered in My Business Account within 2 business days for existing SR&ED claimants, or via a CRA telephone call within 5 business days for new claimants).

Complete and Upload the Application: The applicant completes the application form—entering business details (Lines 010–016), project title, anticipated start date, estimated expenditures, Field of Science or Technology code from Appendix 1 of Guide T4088, technical contact person (Lines 020–032), and a maximum 500-word description on Line 042 of the scientific or technological uncertainty aimed to be addressed—and uploads the application and up to 10 supporting documents in My Business Account under "Submit documents".

Meet with the Assigned Research and Technology Advisor (RTA): The CRA assigns an RTA and schedules a 2-to-5-hour virtual or on-site meeting (mandatory for new claimants; optional at the RTA's request for existing claimants in good standing) to discuss the existing state of knowledge, the scientific or technological uncertainty, the planned systematic investigation, initial hypotheses, and planned experiments or analyses.

Receive Written Evaluation Report Within 8 Weeks: Within 8 weeks of submitting the complete application, the RTA provides a written Pre-Claim Approval evaluation report confirming whether pre-claim approval is granted (valid for up to 3 years).

Submit Form T661 After Undertaking the Work: When the claimant later files its Form T661 (reporting the case number on Lines 212 and 214), claims containing only projects granted Pre-Claim Approval that are selected for an expenditure review benefit from processing service standards cut in half from 180 days to 90 days.

body.text: Separately, if a claimant submits its first SR&ED claim (or has not filed a claim in the last 3 years), the CRA may select it after filing for the mandatory First-Time Claimant Advisory Service (FTCAS). FTCAS is an educational advisory meeting—not a claim review or audit—that provides advice on identifying eligible work, calculating allowable expenditures, and keeping supporting records for future claims, with any expected refund processed after the meeting.
6.4 Statutory Filing Deadlines and the Subsection 220(2.2) Bar on Extensions

Under subsections 37(11) and 127(9)(m) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy, the SR&ED reporting deadline is 12 months after the claimant's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred:

items: Corporations (18 Months): Because a corporation's T2 filing-due date under paragraph 150(1)(a) is 6 months after its taxation year-end, a corporation has 18 months after the end of the taxation year to file Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 (for example, a December 31, 2025 year-end has a T2 due date of June 30, 2026 and an SR&ED reporting deadline of June 30, 2027; a March 31, 2022 year-end had a September 30, 2022 T2 due date and a September 30, 2023 SR&ED deadline). (Exception: A non-profit SR&ED corporation exempt under paragraph 149(1)(j) must file Form T661 by its T2 filing-due date 6 months after year-end under subsection 149(7).)

Individuals / Sole Proprietorships (17.5 Months): Self-employed individuals have 17.5 months after the end of the taxation year (June 15 of the second following year) to file Form T661 and Form T2038(IND).

Partnerships: Form T661 must be filed with the partnership information return no later than 12 months after the earliest of all filing-due dates for the return of income of the members for the taxation year in which the partnership's fiscal period ends.

body.text: If prescribed forms containing the prescribed information are not filed on or before the SR&ED reporting deadline (or the next business day if the deadline falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or CRA-recognized public holiday), subsection 220(2.2) of the Income Tax Act legally prohibits the CRA from granting any time extension. Late-filed expenditures are misclassified under subsection 37(12) and permanently lose all SR&ED deduction and ITC entitlement. Furthermore, once the reporting deadline has passed, a claimant cannot amend its claim to add new projects or substitute additional expenditures to offset costs disallowed by the CRA during a review.
7. CRA Audit Procedures, Claim Review Manual Protocols, and Dispute Resolution
7.1 CRA Processing Service Standards and Joint Technical/Financial Review Protocols

For refundable SR&ED claims (there are no service standards for non-refundable claims), the CRA's published processing service standards from the receipt of a complete claim and income tax return are: 60 days for claims accepted as filed; 90 days for refundable claims selected for review that include only projects granted Pre-Claim Approval; and 180 days for other refundable claims selected for review.

When a claim is selected for review, the examination is governed by the Claim Review Manual (CRM) for Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) and the Financial Claim Review Manual (FCRM) for Financial Reviewers (FRs). Under CRM Chapter 1.5.0 and 1.6.0, the RTA must adhere to due process and the Taxpayer Bill of Rights, coordinate with the FR, prepare a written review plan (identifying the scope, major issues, and methodology), consult the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) whenever unfavourable decisions are contemplated without an on-site visit or when policy questions arise, never negotiate eligibility or expenditures, and organize all working papers in the TF98 file.

Under FCRM Chapter 1 and Chapter 2, the FR has statutory authority to enter a place of business (or a personal residence with the occupant's consent), examine property, inspect and copy books and records, and interview personnel. Crucially, under FCRM Section 2.10.2, while claimants and their authorized representatives may take written notes during a meeting, CRA reviewers must not consent to being recorded by any video or audio recording equipment; if an FR discovers that a claimant is recording a meeting, the reviewer must immediately terminate the meeting and inform the Financial Review Manager (FRM). Before finalizing any adverse adjustments, the RTA and FR issue a written SR&ED review report / proposal package explaining the rationale for the proposed decisions and giving the claimant the opportunity to submit concerns, rebuttals, or additional supporting information.
7.2 Escalation and Formal Dispute Resolution Pathways
If a claimant disagrees with the reviewers' proposed or final determinations, Canadian tax procedure provides four sequential escalation stages:

items: Stage 1 — Assigned Reviewers (RTA / FR): Raise technical or financial concerns directly with the Research and Technology Advisor and/or Financial Reviewer during the review and in response to the proposal package.

Stage 2 — Review Managers (RTM / FRM) and Administrative Second Review: If concerns remain unresolved, escalate to the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) and/or Financial Review Manager (FRM) (and, where due process concerns persist, request an Administrative Second Review) under the Guidelines for Resolving Claimants' SR&ED Concerns.

Stage 3 — Formal Notice of Objection (Subsection 165(1) of the ITA — 90-Day Deadline): After the CRA issues a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment, the claimant may file a formal Notice of Objection under subsection 165(1) of the Income Tax Act within 90 days from the date of the Notice of Assessment or Reassessment.

Stage 4 — Appeal to the Tax Court of Canada and Federal Court of Appeal: If the claimant disagrees with the CRA Appeals Branch's decision on the Notice of Objection, the claimant may file a judicial appeal to the Tax Court of Canada (TCC), with further appeal rights to the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA).

body.text: 8. Landmark Jurisprudence and Judicial Precedents Governing Canadian SR&ED

Canadian courts evaluate SR&ED eligibility through a well-settled line of jurisprudence anchored in the 1998 Tax Court of Canada decision in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. Her Majesty the Queen.
8.1 Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. Her Majesty the Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 D.T.C. 1839 (TCC)

In Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. Her Majesty the Queen ([1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 D.T.C. 1839, [1998] T.C.J. No. 340 (QL)), an engineering consulting firm claimed SR&ED tax credits for hydraulic modelling and river engineering projects that the CRA disallowed as routine engineering. Ruling in favour of the appellant, Judge Donald Bowman (as he then was) set out at paragraph 16 the foundational five criteria (the Five Questions) for determining whether a project qualifies as SR&ED. Judge Bowman established that a project must confront a technological risk or uncertainty that cannot be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures (techniques, procedures, and data generally accessible to competent professionals in the field), formulate and systematically test hypotheses using the scientific method (trained and systematic observation, measurement, experiment, and modification of hypotheses), achieve a technological advancement (which includes proving that a tested hypothesis does not work), and maintain a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results as the work progressed.
8.2 RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen (99 D.T.C. 5087) and C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada (2001 FCA 393)

In RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen ((1998) 99 D.T.C. 5087, 235 N.R. 258, [1998] F.C.J. No. 1890 (QL)), the Federal Court of Appeal (per Justice Robertson, at paragraph 10) formally endorsed Judge Bowman's five-criterion framework from Northwest Hydraulic, holding that repeatability and documentary evidence of systematic testing are vital to establishing that scientific research was undertaken in a systematic fashion. Subsequently, in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada (2001 FCA 393, 2002 D.T.C. 6740), the Federal Court of Appeal at paragraph 17 distilled Northwest Hydraulic and RIS-Christie into the five canonical questions applied across Canadian jurisprudence:

items: Was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures?
Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty?
Did the procedure adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method including the formulation, testing and modification of hypotheses?
Did the process result in a technological advancement?
Was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested, and results kept as the work progressed?

body.text: 8.3 Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. Her Majesty the Queen, 2011 TCC 261, aff'd 2011 FCA 355

In Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. Her Majesty the Queen (2011 TCC 261, affirmed 2011 FCA 355), the appellant plastic sheet thermoformer overhauled its "Multi-Bins" small-parts storage system in fiscal 2005—seeking to increase capacity to 20 cubic feet per square metre, support 100-lb loads on bin fronts, introduce a snap-fit fastenerless design, add modularity, and switch to recyclable plastics—by conducting systematic trials on 8 plastics (PETG, PVC, acrylic, ABS, styrene, Lexan, HDPE, and polyethylene), stands, sliders, and dividers while keeping contemporaneous records. The Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, holding that keeping contemporaneous records of systematic trials does not qualify work as SR&ED when Criterion 1 (technological uncertainty) and Criterion 4 (technological advancement) are absent: manipulating existing thermoforming and injection-moulding processes (such as standard heat sinks and plug-assist techniques) and testing standard commercial plastics to build a better product while controlling costs constituted routine engineering, not SR&ED.
8.4 National R & D Inc. v. Her Majesty the Queen, 2020 TCC 47

In National R & D Inc. v. Her Majesty the Queen (2020 TCC 47, Docket 2017-3837(IT)G), the appellant CCPC claimed $68,029 in SR&ED expenditures ($23,810 ITC) for its 2011 taxation year in developing a web-based Project Tracking System (PTS) using a multi-tiered architecture (ADO, Classic ASP, COM+) and Microsoft SQL Server 2000. Justice Dominique Lafleur held that Criterion 1 (technological uncertainty) was met, ruling that economic and business constraints—being restricted by cost and staff expertise to legacy SQL Server 2000 rather than upgrading to SQL Server 2005—are relevant factors in establishing technological uncertainty within the taxpayer's architecture and business context. However, Justice Lafleur dismissed the appeal because Criteria 2, 3, 4, and 5 were not met: the taxpayer's Project Timeline and table of 50 grouped experiments merely logged hours spent on tasks and vague outcomes without demonstrating how hypotheses were systematically tested and modified as the work progressed.
8.5 Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Her Majesty the Queen, 2021 FCA 88 (aff'g 2019 TCC 246)

In Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Her Majesty the Queen (2021 FCA 88, affirming 2019 TCC 246), the appellant appealed the denial of its 2009 and 2010 SR&ED claims, arguing that because the statutory text of subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act does not explicitly contain the phrase "scientific method", Criterion 3 of Northwest Hydraulic should not have been applied by the Tax Court. Writing for a unanimous Federal Court of Appeal (Webb, Near, and Boivin JJ.A.), Justice Webb rejected the argument, citing Canada Trustco Mortgage Co. v. Canada (2005 SCC 54, para. 10), RIS-Christie, C.W. Agencies, Jentel Manufacturing, and R&D Pro-Innovation Inc. v. Canada (2016 FCA 152), and confirmed that Judge Bowman's five criteria are a settled purposive interpretation of subsection 248(1) and remain binding law.
8.6 Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. The King, 116736 Canada Inc., and Tuna Temple (2026 FCA 175)

In Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. The King (TCC, per Justice Bodie), the taxpayer developed a room-temperature shelf-stable vinegar-based beverage by experimenting with potassium sorbate, sodium benzoate, and Chiber to control microbial growth. Allowing the appeal, Justice Bodie held that (1) technological uncertainty can be established even where a publicly available solution exists, provided it has never been used in that specific context, (2) contemporaneous documentation is meant to track hypotheses, experiments, and results for practitioners in the field and need not be written for someone unfamiliar with the field to replicate the results, and (3) despite the CRA's administrative "Why and How" approach, the five questions from jurisprudence remain a valid and controlling legal methodology. Finally, while 116736 Canada Inc. v. The Queen (98 D.T.C. 1816 (TCC), per Judge Archambault) and Tuna Temple (2026 FCA 175) confirm that the Income Tax Act does not make written reports a statutory prerequisite and that credible, uncontradicted oral testimony is admissible (such as when a fire destroyed records in 116736 Canada Inc.), taxpayers bear the burden of proof on a balance of probabilities across all five Northwest Hydraulic criteria.

Interpretation of SR&ED definition in river hydraulic modelling.
Taxpayer won. Established at para. 16 the 5 foundational criteria for SR&ED, defined "routine engineering," and held that disproving a hypothesis is a technological advancement.

Repeatability and documentary proof of systematic testing.
Crown won. Endorsed Northwest Hydraulic at appellate level; held that repeatability and documentary evidence of testing are central to proving systematic research.
116736 Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 98 D.T.C. 1816
Admissibility of oral testimony when written records were destroyed by fire.
Taxpayer won. Held that the ITA does not require written reports as a legal prerequisite; credible oral testimony can establish SR&ED.
Data Kinetics Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 D.T.C. 1877
Whether dedicated telecom bandwidth and mainframe access qualify as leased equipment under the Proxy Method.
Taxpayer won. Held that dedicated bandwidth/mainframe leasing constitutes a lease of sophisticated optoelectronic equipment (not GPOEF)—adopted in CRA's June 8, 2026 Lease Expenditures Policy.
C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393, 2002 D.T.C. 6740
Formulation of the 5-part judicial test for SR&ED eligibility.
Crown won. Summarized Northwest Hydraulic and RIS-Christie at para. 17 into the canonical Five Questions applied in all subsequent Canadian SR&ED cases.
Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 TCC 261, aff'd 2011 FCA 355
Distinction between SR&ED and routine thermoforming / product design.
Crown won. Held that systematic testing of known plastics and standard moulding techniques is routine engineering, even when supported by contemporaneous records.
Application of the 5 criteria to industrial development claims.
Crown won. Reaffirmed at para. 4 that the five criteria of Northwest Hydraulic govern SR&ED determinations.
National R & D Inc. v. The Queen, 2020 TCC 47
Software development under legacy constraints (SQL Server 2000) and adequacy of task logs.

Crown won. Held that economic/legacy constraints can establish technological uncertainty (Criterion 1 met), but time-tracking logs and grouped trial tables without hypothesis modification failed Criteria 2–5.
Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, 2021 FCA 88 (aff'g 2019 TCC 246)
Challenge to Criterion 3 ("scientific method") following relocation of s. 248(1) definition to the ITA.
Crown won. Unanimously held that Judge Bowman's 5 criteria are a binding purposive interpretation of subsection 248(1) under Canada Trustco.
Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. The King
Food-science experimentation using known preservatives in a novel context.

Taxpayer won. Held that known solutions applied in an untested context can create technological uncertainty, documentation need not be written for laypersons, and the 5 questions remain valid alongside CRA's "Why and How" test.
